analysis.one_liner: Bans coal companies from promising their own word instead of real money to cover mine cleanup.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House committee: it was referred to the Natural Resources Committee in March 2017 and sent to a subcommittee, and no hearing or vote ever happened before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a coal company digs a mine, federal law requires it to post money up front to restore the land afterward. Some companies instead post a "self-bond" — a promise backed by their own financial strength — and when those companies go bankrupt, the cleanup bill falls to taxpayers. This bill would ban new self-bonds, require existing ones to be replaced with real bonds backed by a surety company or collateral, and bar companies from using coal mines or worthless mining assets as that collateral.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers in mining states, who otherwise absorb cleanup costs when a self-bonded coal company collapses, and residents of mining communities who live near unreclaimed mines.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the federal Office of Surface Mining and Reclamation Enforcement and state regulators from accepting new self-bonds for coal mine reclamation, so cleanup money must come from a real bond rather than a company's promise.

Requires existing self-bonds and corporate surety bonds to be converted to surety or collateral bonds — at permit renewal or major permit modification at the latest — so past promises get replaced with enforceable financial backing.

Bars coal, mines, mine land, coal waste sites, and mining equipment without resale value from serving as bond collateral, closing the loophole of a company securing its cleanup obligation with the very assets that would be worthless if it failed.

Directs rules limiting how many reclamation bonds any one surety company can issue in a state and requiring minimum collateralization, so the cleanup guarantee itself does not become a new source of collapse risk.

analysis.who_pays: Coal companies that currently self-bond, which would have to buy surety bonds or post cash and other qualifying collateral, tightening credit for marginal operators.

drawbacks.text: Buying real surety bonds or posting collateral costs money, and for financially struggling coal companies that added expense could hasten bankruptcies or mine closures, with job losses in already-pressed coal communities.

If surety companies refuse to bond distressed operators, those companies would have to post cash or property immediately, which the bill's own collateral restrictions make harder, so some marginal mines could lose the ability to operate at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill shifts a real, demonstrated risk — bankrupt coal companies leaving taxpayers the cleanup bill — from the public onto the companies creating it, and it adds rules so the surety industry does not become a new weak link. The honest cost is that it squeezes marginal coal operators, which could mean closures and job losses in coal towns, though those are precisely the companies most likely to leave their cleanup unfunded.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee from April 2017 until the Congress ended in January 2019 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on March 30, 2017 with 28 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources on the day of introduction.
On April 11, 2017 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it remained for the rest of the 115th Congress.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal companies that self-bond kept the ability to back their cleanup obligations with their own word, leaving the risk of abandoned-mine cleanup costs with taxpayers rather than the industry.

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Coal Cleanup Taxpayer Protection Act on March 30, 2017.

for.name: 33 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all recorded cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Rep. Rob Bishop
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill, which stayed in his committee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Coal mining companies using self-bonds
against.what_they_did: Benefited from self-bonding and opposed restrictions on it during this period, when several large self-bonded coal producers had recently gone through bankruptcy.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 33 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would end self-bonding and force companies to buy real bonds or post qualifying collateral, shifting cleanup risk back onto the industry. The companies that benefit most from self-bonding are those least able to cover their own reclamation costs.

Requiring every coal operator to carry a surety or collateral bond creates a large new market for corporate sureties. The bill adds rules capping their exposure per state and requiring minimum collateralization so they do not become the next point of failure.
